source.title: NeuronScope: A Multi-Agent Framework for Explaining Polysemantic Neurons in Language Models
source.authors: Wei-Qi Liu; Yongliang Miao; Hai-Yan Zhao; Yan-Guang Liu; Mengnan Du

page_placements.theme: Language-model neurons often carry several behaviours or lack a clean label

record.file_problem: No apparent file problem; the full paper text, including appendices, is present.
record.tranche_reason: It evaluates neuron explanations by predicting activations on held-out text, a different measure from the claim’s audit of neuron-pole job shares. This bears on V7’s automated-scoring version.
record.gate_note: The paper reports activation-prediction scores and semantic-concept counts for a refinement ablation, plus a score-convergence figure. The qualitative comparison with another explanation method in Appendix H does not report a numerical result about the claim’s object and is not separately rowed. The reported semantic counts do not measure the share of poles with one or two jobs.
record.test_reason: This is a method paper (NeuronScope). It uses simulator-based activation-correlation scoring as its optimisation target and metric, and reports only its own pipeline against its own no-refinement ablation. It reports mean scores, never the share of neurons with good scores, so it does not test V7. It does not audit job shares (V1/V2) or address V3–V6.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right, with one correction. The quantitative comparison is only against NeuronScope's own no-refinement variant. The claimed superiority over 'single-pass baselines' (Choi et al.-style descriptions) rests on qualitative examples in Appendix H/Table 3, with no reported scores.
record.recipe_differences: The study uses a multi-agent decomposition, clustering, and iterative-refinement pipeline scored by a fine-tuned activation simulator, rather than auditing the claimed Qwen3-32B neuron-pole job proportions.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported score varies by model and layer. The refinement comparison shows higher scores in every listed model-layer setting; the convergence analysis reports diminishing improvement after approximately five iterations.

fits_no_version.finding: For the 200 most frequently active neurons per layer, LLM decomposition plus HDBSCAN clustering yields on average 2.2–2.5 explanation clusters per neuron in Gemma-2-2B and Qwen3-4B, and 4.5–5.5 in Llama-3.1-8B. The clusters are often rephrasings of related triggers (e.g. several '#'/code-comment variants).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: An automated decomposition pipeline assigns multiple semantic clusters to most frequently active LLM neurons, but the cluster count is not validated as counting distinct jobs.

fits_no_version.finding: Mean per-cluster simulator correlation is 0.33–0.66 across models and layers. Refinement adds about 0.05–0.10 in every setting.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Iterative activation-feedback refinement modestly raises simulator-scored explanation quality for selected neurons.

record.problems: The paper reports no uncertainty estimates for Table 1. It does not define a good-score threshold or report the fraction of neurons above one, and the convergence figure’s exact scores are not stated in the text. The authors note computational overhead and possible sensitivity to the quality and diversity of activation samples.
record.rows_left_out: Appendix H’s qualitative comparison with another explanation method is not rowed because it reports descriptions rather than a numerical result about the claim’s object. The qualitative clustering examples and figures are not separately rowed because they do not measure the shares specified in the claim versions.

untested.parts: No Qwen3-32B audit and no share of poles with one or two jobs.
No job-share figures for any model. Only small dense models (2B–8B) are examined, with no MoE or very large models.
No vision models and no InceptionV1 examples.
No comparison of architectures or regularisation, and no estimate of interpretable share.
There is no comparison of explanations fitted to top-activating examples against prediction on broader text.
No fraction of neurons with good simulation scores, and no scoring on random or unselected text. There is only a mean correlation for a selected neuron subset.

record.verdict_notes: The relation is downgraded from tests/T2 to uses_without_test/T4: simulator scoring is the optimisation objective and metric, and every number is about the method's own performance. Neuron selection by activation frequency, per-cluster scoring on exemplar subsets, and a fine-tuned Llama-3.1-8B simulator make the scores incomparable with Bills et al. No uncertainty is reported.

versions.untested_parts: The study does not audit Qwen3-32B neuron poles or report proportions with one job, two related jobs, or unexplained poles.

It studies three smaller models and reports semantic-concept counts and explanation scores, not the claimed shares across models, dense and mixture-of-experts architectures, or trillion-parameter models.
No InceptionV1 cat-and-car example or recursive-generalization account is tested.
It does not test the proposed architecture, regularization, and tool explanations for interpretability or estimate interpretability shares in vision models.
It does not evaluate attribution graphs or compare neuron-based circuits with a trained replacement model.
Although it scores predictions on held-out text, it does not test whether an explanation fitted to activating examples fails to predict firing elsewhere.
It reports simulator-based activation-correlation scores on held-out text, but does not define a threshold for a “good” score or report the fraction of neurons above such a threshold.

rows.subject: Llama-3.1-8b
rows.operation_detail: Score explanations by simulator-predicted activation correlation on held-out text, comparing NeuronScope with its no-refinement variant.
rows.measure: Neuron-level Score (Pearson correlation between predicted and true activations)
rows.note: The paper does not specify what score qualifies as good, so this result cannot establish the share of neurons with good scores.
rows.check: These are the study's own method against its own ablation, reported as means over the 200 most frequently active neurons per layer (Appendix B), so not a representative sample. Score(E, Dk) is computed per semantic cluster on 'a held-out set of text exemplars', likely activating exemplars rather than random text. No share above any threshold is given, so the rows cannot show whether only a minority of neurons score well.

rows.subject: Llama-3.1-8b
rows.operation_detail: Compare the Number of semantic concepts associated with a neuron under NeuronScope and its no-refinement variant.
rows.note: The paper says this metric remains unchanged; it is a concept count, not a proportion of neuron poles with a given number of jobs.
rows.check: The Number metric is identical by construction, since both arms share the decomposition and clustering stages. 'Observed' has no meaning here: it is a design invariant, not an effect. The values themselves (mean 2.2–5.5 LLM-derived explanation clusters per neuron) are a related construct, not V1's audited pole-job shares.

rows.subject: Llama-3.1-8b
rows.operation_detail: Track simulator-based explanation Score over five refinement iterations; report mean scores across sampled neurons.

conditions.value: four layers; layer indices not stated in the text describing this analysis
five randomly sampled neurons per layer

rows.note: The text says scores rise during early iterations and improvements become marginal after approximately five iterations, but gives no score values. It does not determine the fraction of neurons with good scores.
rows.check: Figure-only result on 5 neurons × 4 Llama layers. It shows only that the study's own refinement converges, with no readable values and no share of neurons scoring well.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.

relation.reason: Simulator-based activation-correlation scoring is the study's optimisation target and its metric. It reports no share of well-scored neurons and tests no version.

tranche.reason: Method paper. It reports only its own pipeline against its own no-refinement ablation, so no version of the claim is tested.

source_check.notes: Number is identical in both arms by design ('remains unchanged across all settings'). Superiority over single-pass baselines is shown only by qualitative examples (App. H, Table 3), with no baseline scores. Refinement keeps the highest-scoring of 8 candidates per iteration on held-out data. The text names no test split apart from the validation split (App. C), so the refinement gains may include selection on the evaluation set.

statements.correction: This study's subjects are Llama-3.1-8B, Gemma-2-2B and Qwen3-4B (Table 2), none above 10B. Its only Qwen rows are Qwen3-4b (Table 1). The simulator is a fine-tuned Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct. It is a method paper, not a V7 test.

Table 1, layer 5: Llama 0.453/0.508, Gemma 0.600/0.663, Qwen 0.489/0.589. Llama layer 10: 0.334/0.390. The 200 neurons per layer are those with the highest activation frequency, not a random sample (App. B). Score is Pearson correlation on a held-out validation split (App. C).
statements.problem: The numbers match Table 1. The 0.13-0.18 Gemma 2 comparison comes from other studies and was not checked here.

statements.correction: Table 1 Number: Gemma 2.22-2.49, Qwen 2.26-2.42, Llama 4.48-5.53. Uses the 200 neurons per layer with the highest activation frequency. GPT-4o decomposition, then text-embedding-3-small plus HDBSCAN, min cluster size 2 (App. B).
